{"id": "08952ddb-b26c-42a9-b127-1061767b7e2f", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_35A19nBn3yJAeIcu1qqxg6", "content": "[{'text': '## Documentation search results\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Understanding and Remediating Cold Starts: An AWS Lambda Perspective | AWS Compute Blog\",\"context\":\"### SnapStart\\\\n\\\\nLambda SnapStart improves cold invoke latency by reducing the time it takes for a function to initialize and become ready to handle incoming requests. When SnapStart is enabled for a function, Lambda creates an encrypted snapshot of the initialized execution environment when you publish a new function version. This triggers an optimized INIT phase of the function where an immutable, encrypted snapshot of the memory and disk is taken. This snapshot is cached for reuse later. When a SnapStart-enabled function is invoked again, Lambda restores the execution environment from the cached snapshot instead of creating a new environment, thus moderating a cold invoke. SnapStart minimizes the invocation latency of a function, since creating a new execution environment no longer requires a dedicated INIT phase.\\\\n\\\\nSnapStart is an efficient cold start solution, currently available for Java, Python, and .NET functions. It is particularly useful for functions with long initialization times. Inactive snapshots are automatically removed after after 14 days without invocation for Java based runtimes. For detailed pricing information, check out our pricing page.\\\\n\\\\n[](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/1b6453892473a467d07372d45eb05abc2031647a/2025/08/06/image-3-9.jpeg)\\\\n\\\\nFigure 3: Lambda SnapStart architecture: optimizing cold starts through snapshot-based initialization\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/understanding-and-remediating-cold-starts-an-aws-lambda-perspective/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Understanding Lambda Event Function scaling\",\"context\":\"### Provisioned concurrency\\\\n\\\\nYou use reserved concurrency to define the maximum number of execution environments reserved for a Lambda Event Function.\\\\nHowever, none of these environments come pre-initialized. As a result, your Event Function invocations might take longer\\\\nbecause Lambda must first initialize the new environment before being able to use it to invoke your Event Function.\\\\nWhen Lambda has to initialize a new environment to carry out an invocation, this is known as a\\\\ncold start.\\\\nTo mitigate cold starts, you can use provisioned concurrency.\\\\n\\\\nProvisioned concurrency is the number of pre-initialized execution environments that you want to allocate to\\\\nyour Event Function. If you set provisioned concurrency on an Event Function, Lambda initializes that number of execution\\\\nenvironments so that they are prepared to respond immediately to Event Function requests.\\\\n\\\\n**Note:**\\\\n\\\\nUsing provisioned concurrency incurs additional charges to your account. If you\\'re working with the Java\\\\n11 or Java 17 runtimes, you can also use Lambda SnapStart to mitigate cold start issues at no additional cost.\\\\nSnapStart uses cached snapshots of your execution environment to significantly improve startup\\\\nperformance. You cannot use both SnapStart and provisioned concurrency on the same Event Function version. For more\\\\ninformation about SnapStart features, limitations, and supported Regions, see Improving startup performance with Lambda SnapStart.\\\\n\\\\nWhen using provisioned concurrency, Lambda still recycles execution environments in the background. For example,\\\\nthis can occur after an invocation failure. However, at\\\\nany given time, Lambda always ensures that the number of pre-initialized environments is equal to the value of your\\\\nEvent Function\\'s provisioned concurrency setting. Importantly, even if you\\'re using provisioned concurrency, you can\\\\nstill experience a cold start delay if Lambda has to reset the execution environment.\\\\n\\\\nIn contrast, when using reserved concurrency, Lambda might completely terminate an environment after a period of\\\\ninactivity. The following diagram illustrates this by comparing the lifecycle of a single execution environment\\\\nwhen you configure your Event Function using reserved concurrency compared to provisioned concurrency.\\\\n\\\\nThe diagram has four points of interest:\\\\n\\\\n| Time | Reserved concurrency | Provisioned concurrency |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| t1 | Nothing happens. | Lambda pre-initializes an execution environment instance. |\\\\n| t2 | Request 1 comes in. Lambda must initialize a new execution environment instance. | Request 1 comes in. Lambda uses the pre-initialized environment instance. |\\\\n| t3 | After some inactivity, Lambda terminates the active environment instance\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot Lambda function cold start issues?\",\"context\":\"### Long INIT duration in provisioned concurrency\\\\n\\\\n[For on-demand Lambda functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html#optimizing-latency), the static initializer runs after a request is received but before the handler is invoked. This results in latency for the requester and contributes to the cold start duration.\\\\n\\\\nTake the following actions:\\\\n\\\\n* Find out whether your function exceeds the configured level of provisioned concurrency. On the **Metrics** page of the [CloudWatch console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/), check the [ProvisionedConcurrencySpilloverInvocations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/monitoring-metrics-types.html#invocation-metrics) metric to find the number of times your Lambda function invoked with standard concurrency. A non-zero value means that all provisioned concurrency is in use and invocation occurred with a cold start.\\\\n* If you get cold starts after you active provisioned concurrency, then see [Lambda: Cold starts with provisioned concurrency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/troubleshooting-invocation.html#troubleshooting-invocation-coldstart)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/lambda-cold-start\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. {"id": "2623a43a-4c66-4504-bbad-3737cfe54982", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "This is the classic Lambda **cold start** pattern, and it's expected behavior, not a bug:

**Why it happens:**
- Lambda tears down idle execution environments after a period of inactivity. When the next request arrives after that quiet window, Lambda has to spin up a brand-new environment — download/mount your code, start the runtime, and run your function's initialization code (imports, SDK clients, DB connections, etc.) — *before* it can even start your handler.
- That init work happens inline on the first request, which is why it's visibly slower than subsequent "warm" invokes that reuse an already-initialized environment.
- Heavier runtimes/packages (large deployment packages, many SDK clients, VPC-attached ENIs) tend to make this worse.

**Ways to mitigate it:**
- **Provisioned concurrency** — keeps a set number of environments pre-initialized and ready, so requests skip the init phase entirely (costs extra, always-on).
- **SnapStart** — available for Java, Python, and .NET functions. Lambda snapshots the initialized environment after you publish a version and restores from that snapshot on a cold invoke instead of running init from scratch. No additional cost, but the snapshot gets removed after 14 days without invocation (for Java).
- Reducing init-time work (lazy-load SDK clients, trim dependencies, avoid unnecessary VPC attachment) also shrinks the cold start itself.

If you'd like, I can check your actual functions in `eu-central-1` — their init duration, memory size, VPC config, and whether provisioned concurrency/SnapStart is already enabled — to confirm cold starts are the cause and see which mitigation would help most.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
